pages.original_text:
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 In a speech earlier this

year, I explored scenarios in which artificial intelligence (AI) could affect economic

inequality, for better or for worse.2 My focus in those remarks was on the AI side of this

relationship, and today I would like to return to this topic by first providing some

important context about inequality in the United States.

        Inequality is an aspect of every economy, and understanding the extent and

evolution of inequality in the United States can help in forming a clear view of the

economic outlook and how the economy is likely to react to new developments.

Widening inequality may also, depending on many factors, reflect a decline in economic

opportunity for many people, which can limit the economy’s productive capacity.

        Today, I will begin by summarizing the current state of economic inequality in the

United States, assisted by new results from a long-running survey of households

conducted by the Federal Reserve, and then show where this fits into the history of

inequality over the past century or so. I will explore some of the forces that have shaped

inequality, and what these forces may indicate about how AI is likely to affect the way

wealth and income are distributed.

Wealth and Income Inequality Today

        Up-to-date and detailed information about inequality in the United States comes

from the latest edition of the Federal Reserve’s triennial Survey of Consumer Finances,

conducted in 2025 and published just last month.3 The survey confirms that both wealth

格差はどの経済にもあります。米国での格差の程度と変化を理解すれば、景気の見通しと、新たな出来事に経済がどう反応するかが見えやすくなります。条件によっては、格差の拡大が多くの人の経済機会の減少を反映し、経済の生産能力を制約することもあります。

        Wealth concentration has increased at the very top. Using Forbes magazine’s

tally of the 400 wealthiest individuals, together with data from the Survey of Consumer

Finances, a rough estimate is that their share of total wealth rose from 3 percent in 2022

to 4 percent in the most recent survey. Forbes counts nearly 1,000 U.S. billionaires.6

        Digging into the sources of widening inequality, the wealth of those at the top is

primarily held in the form of business assets. Research using data from the Survey of

Consumer Finances back to the 1940s shows that returns on business equity have been a

major source of widening wealth inequality over the decades.7 Most of the income for

these wealthy households is in capital income—interest, dividends, capital gains, and

business profits—rather than wages and salaries. Unlike these higher-income or

wealthier households, most income for middle-class households comes from their

paychecks. And it’s harder to build wealth that way.

        Although the largest asset class for wealthy households is typically stocks and

other financial assets, a substantial amount of their capital income also comes from

ownership of private businesses. These private businesses come in two broad types: an

actively managed business—such as a plumbing business, retail store, or manufacturing

firm—and a passive investment in a business, commonly known as private equity.

         Economic research suggests three causes of the decades-long trend in labor versus

capital income, each highly relevant to the potential effects of AI on inequality. The first

is technological innovations that have reduced demand for labor and decreased wages;

the second is the concentration of market power in many industries with a small number

of firms; and the third related cause is the reduction in the bargaining power of workers.

         Technology replacing labor has been going on for centuries, but new technology

can also augment the productivity of existing jobs and create new jobs, including those

that are hard to envision when the technology is initially adopted, a point I have noted in

a number of speeches.17 The internet and the businesses it created reduced employment
